# Engagement quality (LO6)

*How well did you collaborate with AI?*

This chapter summarizes the **LO6: AI-Augmented Learning** framework from the Fontys *AI for Society* minor — useful for coaches, assessors, and ICT professionals who want a shared vocabulary for AI-augmented learning.

Narrative and colleague-session guide: [AI-Augmented Learning](ai.augmented.learning01.qmd).

## The learning outcome

> You use conversational AI to learn, plan, critique, and reflect. You set boundaries, cite AI contributions, and demonstrate growth over time.

We **require** conversational AI use and evidence of process — not avoidance. For LO6, **"AI" means conversational AI** (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot), not building models (that is a different learning outcome).

## Two students revisited

Same deliverable, different growth. Student A **accepted** output; Student B **integrated** AI with their own thinking and left a trail. Assessment must look beyond polish:

> If we only assess the document, we assess ChatGPT — not the student.

The only way to know whether someone understands their work is **ongoing conversation** across tasks and time. AI makes skipping that conversation impossible.

## Quantity vs quality

The [MMM label system](https://mmmlabel.tech/) (Lazy Prompter → Man-Made) measures **how much** AI was involved — valuable for transparency. It can smuggle in a hidden norm: less AI = more authentic = better.

LO6 asks a different question:

| MMM-style | LO6-style |
|-----------|-----------|
| How much AI did you use? | How well did you collaborate with AI? |
| Quantity | Quality |
| Less AI = better (implicit) | Conscious engagement (explicit) |

Students need skills for **how and when** to collaborate, an ethical compass, and the ability to **articulate their choices** — not shame for using tools that are already everywhere in professional life.

## Four levels of engagement

These describe **processes**, not fixed identities. Someone may Integrate on Monday and Accept on Tuesday — that is fine if they **notice** and recover when the task demands more.

| Level | Name | Investment | What it looks like |
|:-----:|------|------------|-------------------|
| 1 | **Accepting** | Minimal | Taking output at face value; copy-paste with surface edits |
| 2 | **Refining** | Moderate | Adjusting and polishing; core ideas unchanged |
| 3 | **Challenging** | Significant | Pushing back, verifying, fact-checking, documenting disagreements |
| 4 | **Integrating** | Deep | Combining AI input with own thinking; original insights emerge |

**Calibrating:** A student who says they were *Challenging* because they "Googled whether numbers seemed reasonable" may be *Refining with good intentions*. Help them see what actual Challenging would require — that is learning, not punishment.

Know when Accepting is enough (quick fact lookup) and when Integrating is required (complex analysis). Be honest about the difference.

## Patterns to recognize

| Pattern | What you observe | What may be happening | Try asking |
|---------|------------------|----------------------|------------|
| Hiding use | Polish, vague "I used AI a bit", can't explain reasoning | Shame, fear, or Accepting without awareness | Walk me through your process — where did *you* decide? |
| Receipts only | Long prompt logs, no reflection | Documentation mistaken for engagement | Where did you disagree or learn something new? |
| Avoiding AI | Struggle on tasks AI could scaffold | AI seen as cheating or threatening | What if AI challenged your ideas instead of writing them? |
| Growing collaboration | Dialogue trail; can separate contributions | This is what we want | What made you push back on X? |
| Regressing under pressure | Early Integrating, late Accepting when rushed | Deadlines; human, but needs noticing | What happened? How might you handle that differently next time? |
| Outsourcing the thinking | Polished portfolio or report; cannot recall or explain own text after time away | Accepting at scale — deliverable done, learning skipped | What do you still own? What would recovery look like (messy notes first, AI as memory not author)? |

See also the [portfolio story](ai.augmented.learning01.qmd#keeping-control-a-portfolio-story) and [notes-first section](ai.augmented.learning01.qmd#your-notes-first-mind-maps-handwriting-and-memory) in chapter 1 — encoding while you listen matters as much as who polishes the final text.

## Growth is messy

A realistic trajectory — not a straight line:

- Week 2: Integrating (excited, experimenting)
- Week 4: Accepting (deadline pressure)
- Week 6: Challenging (feedback landed)
- Week 8: Accepting (project chaos)
- Week 10: Integrating (breakthrough)
- Week 14: Integrating (pulled it together)

What matters: Can they **notice** slipping into Accepting when higher engagement is needed? **Recover** when the task demands it? **Articulate** what they learned?

## What "proficient" looks like

A proficient learner (student or professional):

- Knows the difference between Accepting and Integrating
- Chooses consciously based on the task
- Documents process — not only prompts
- Explains what they learned vs what AI contributed
- Reflects honestly on shortcuts

They do not need to be brilliant at prompting. They need to be **in the driver's seat**.

## Proficiency scale (LO6)

| Scale | What it looks like |
|-------|-------------------|
| **Undefined** | No evidence of collaboration; avoids or hides use; cannot discuss process |
| **Orienting** | Uses AI without awareness; mostly Accepting; "I used ChatGPT" is the whole reflection |
| **Beginning** | Developing awareness; occasional Challenging or Integrating; starting to notice patterns |
| **Proficient** | Consistent conscious choice; articulates why; integrates when needed; honest about shortcuts |
| **Advanced** | Sophisticated integration; models practice for others; connects collaboration to societal impact |

## LO6 alongside other outcomes

LO6 is judged **in context** with the rest of the minor — same idea applies in professional teams:

| Focus | LO6 shows up as… |
|-------|------------------|
| Societal impact | Did AI widen perspectives — or narrow them? |
| Needs analysis | Verified suggestions — or accepted the first list? |
| Model interaction | Challenged outputs when building with AI? |
| Professional standard | How was AI used in stakeholder communication? |
| Personal leadership | Can they reflect on their own AI patterns? |

## Coaches: learn alongside

Most of us are still at a basic level with our own AI use. That is okay.

We have judged students for technologies we did not yet understand — calculators, Wikipedia, Google, Stack Overflow. Each time the tool became normal; each time we eventually taught **how to use it well** instead of **whether to use it at all**.

AI is this generation's moment. The invitation: **learn alongside your students**. Notice your own patterns. Curiosity models exactly what we ask of them.

## Quick reference

1. **Quality over quantity** — how well they collaborated, not how much AI they used
2. **Process over polish** — dialogue documentation beats glossy output
3. **Calibrate, don't catch** — help them understand the standard
4. **Growth is messy** — awareness and recovery, not a straight line
5. **You are learning too** — model curiosity

### Questions that work

| Situation | Try asking |
|-----------|------------|
| Vague about AI use | Walk me through your process. Where did AI help? Where did you push back? |
| Polished output, no documentation | This looks great — I can't see your thinking. How did you get here? |
| Avoided AI | What stopped you? What would you try if you did use it? |
| Self-assessment seems inflated | You said Challenging — show me the evidence. |
| Student struggling | AI can help you think, not just produce. What if it critiqued your ideas? |
| Student shows growth | I see your engagement deepened. What changed? |
